title: The Kyoto Card Shop Whose First Year No One Can Prove
dek: Nintendo says Fusajiro Yamauchi began making flower cards in Kyoto in 1889; the paper trail is thinner than the cards he left behind.

story.event: Starting a hanafuda card business in Kyoto's crowded card-making quarter
story.summary: Nintendo dates its beginning to 1889, when Fusajiro Yamauchi began making and selling hanafuda flower cards in Shimogyo, Kyoto, in a neighbourhood of more than thirty card wholesalers. Historians describe a small side business making high-end decks such as the Napoleon-branded Daitoryo line; Yamauchi retired in 1929 and handed the company to his son-in-law Sekiryo. The card researcher Marcus Richert found that early business directories give the founding year as 1892 and that the earliest record of Fusajiro he could find dates from 1895.
paragraphs: Nintendo's official history begins with one line: in 1889, Fusajiro Yamauchi started making and selling hanafuda in Shimogyo, Kyoto. Hanafuda are small, stiff flower cards with twelve suits, one for each month of the year. It was a crowded trade. The playing-card researcher Marcus Richert counts more than thirty card wholesalers in the Shomendori and Takasegawa neighbourhood where the shop stood.

Nor was it respectable. Under the Tokugawa shogunate playing cards had been banned, and hanafuda kept a reputation as a gambler's deck. By the 1880s the Meiji government had softened its position; one account dates the change to 1885. Yamauchi, born a Fukui and adopted into the Yamauchi family, left no interview or memoir explaining his choice. The historian Florent Gorges has said Yamauchi liked to play cards for money with friends and wondered why Kyoto, a pleasure city, could not support a card-making business. Another historian, Alexander Smith, describes the start as a side business in a small building, perhaps a dozen artisans making cards by hand.

Yamauchi aimed at the top of the market. His first set, the Daitoryo or 'president' line, carried Napoleon Bonaparte on the cover and was made for gambling houses and buyers with money to spare. In 1902, by Nintendo's account, the company became the first in Japan to make Western-style playing cards, and over the following decades it became one of Japan's largest card makers. In 1929 Yamauchi retired, handing the business to Sekiryo, husband of his daughter Tei.

What is odd is how little paper the beginning left. Searching Japan's National Diet Library, Richert found business directories from the 1910s and 1920s that give the founding year as 1892; the first mention of 1889 he found was a 1936 entry for Sekiryo. The earliest record of Fusajiro he has seen dates from 1895, and he registered no trademark until 1900. A photograph long shared as the 1889 shop shows a bicycle that bicycle historians date to between 1912 and 1930. Even the meaning of the name Nintendo, his great-grandson Hiroshi Yamauchi later admitted, has been lost.
The cards lasted better than the records. In October 2024 Nintendo opened its first museum in a former card factory in Kyoto, with a workshop where visitors make their own hanafuda.

quote.text: That is musk which discloses itself by its smell, and not what the perfumers impose upon us:--If a man be expert in any art he needs not tell it, for his own skill will show it.
quote.locator: Chapter VIII, "Of the Duties of Society", maxim LXI
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Yamauchi left no account of himself, and the documents that might have told his story say little or contradict one another. Saadi suggests that was never the test: a craftsman's skill shows in what he makes, as musk shows by its scent rather than by the seller's claims.

reflection: You work in a field where a result that was not recorded might as well not exist, so this story may sit oddly with you. Yamauchi left almost no paper, and his company still cannot say for certain which year it began. Yet the thing he made held its shape for more than a century.

Most of the days you spend building something will not be written down by anyone, and the ones that matter may not feel like beginnings while you are in them. Saadi's point is a gentle one. You do not have to announce the care you take. It shows to the person who picks up what you made.
invitation: Choose one small thing you will hand to someone today, perhaps a reply or a short note, and make it as clear as you can without mentioning how much effort it took.

cross_checks.claim: Fusajiro Yamauchi began making hanafuda in Kyoto, a beginning Nintendo dates to 1889
Fusajiro was not born a Yamauchi but was adopted into the Yamauchi family
Playing cards had been banned under the Tokugawa shogunate, and hanafuda were associated with gambling
In 1929 the business passed to Sekiryo, husband of Fusajiro's daughter Tei

research_notes: Founding date: Nintendo, Film Stories, I Programmer and AFP all give 1889 (Wikipedia gives 23 September 1889, another account 6 November). Marcus Richert's research in the National Diet Library (TechRadar) found Taisho and early Showa directories consistently giving 1892, the first 1889 mention in a 1936 entry for Sekiryo, and no record of Fusajiro before 1895. The story gives Nintendo's date as Nintendo's and reports Richert's findings as his; it does not decide between them. Richert also says Fusajiro would have been 21 in 1889, while I Programmer and Wikipedia give a birth year of 1859, which would make him about 30; the story gives no age. Legalisation of cards: Film Stories gives 1885; another search result described the Meiji change as gradual toleration rather than a single repeal, so the story says the government had softened its position by the 1880s and attributes the 1885 date to 'one account'. Motive: no first-hand statement by Yamauchi exists; the story attributes the gambling-with-friends account to the historian Florent Gorges and the side-business description to Alexander Smith, both as quoted in Film Stories. Film Stories also says Fusajiro had run the family cement firm Haiko Honten and worked on the Lake Biwa Canal; SuperJump repeats the cement claim citing the City of Kyoto, but neither is first-hand, so the story leaves it out. The often-repeated deal to sell cards through Japan Tobacco and Salt Public Corporation shops is omitted: that corporation dates from 1949 and the claim could not be sourced reliably. An Unseen Japan article was not used because its reference list cites a 1907 'Kyoto Commercial Archives' title that could not be traced. Scale: TechRadar says the company would become the largest card maker in Japan without saying when; Film Stories says one of the largest; the story uses the conservative wording. The Saadi maxim is applied by analogy; it is a general saying about skill speaking for itself.
